lesson.title: Untangling dy/dx: The Algebra After the Calculus
lesson.summary: Once an equation is differentiated, dy/dx often appears in more than one term; isolating it is a separate, purely algebraic skill worth practicing on its own.
lesson.body:
Differentiating an implicit equation is only half the job. The result almost never comes out with dy/dx already alone on one side; instead it shows up multiplied by different expressions in two or more separate terms, and getting from there to a usable formula for dy/dx is a specific algebraic routine worth isolating as its own skill: move every term containing dy/dx to one side of the equation and every other term to the other side, factor dy/dx out of the terms that contain it, then divide.

Take x^2 y + y^3 = 5, and check the point (2, 1) first: 2^2 (1) + 1^3 = 4 + 1 = 5, so it lies on the curve. Differentiate term by term. The term x^2 y is a product of x^2 and y(x), so it needs the product rule: d/dx[x^2 y] = x^2 (dy/dx) + 2xy. The term y^3 needs the chain rule: d/dx[y^3] = 3y^2 (dy/dx). The right side is d/dx[5] = 0. So:

x^2 (dy/dx) + 2xy + 3y^2 (dy/dx) = 0

Now do the algebra. Move the term without dy/dx to the right side: x^2 (dy/dx) + 3y^2 (dy/dx) = -2xy. Factor dy/dx out of the left side: (dy/dx)(x^2 + 3y^2) = -2xy. Divide by the factor: dy/dx = -2xy/(x^2 + 3y^2). At (2, 1): dy/dx = -2(2)(1)/(4 + 3) = -4/7.

Two mistakes are worth watching for at this stage. First, forgetting the product rule on a mixed term like x^2 y, and treating it as if only one factor depended on x. Second, sign errors when moving terms across the equals sign, especially when dy/dx appears with a positive coefficient in one term and would need to combine with a negative one elsewhere. Slowing down for this algebraic cleanup step is what turns a correctly differentiated equation into an actual formula for the slope.
